incident_description: My  14" electric chainsaw made by Chicago electric power tools and sold by Harbor Freight Tools Model # 67255 suddenly would not shut off when the trigger switch was released. This created a very dangerous situation in which I had stop the saw by stepping on the extension cord and pulling the saw loose at the electrical connection. I took the saw apart and saw that the trigger switch, a small micro switch,wasnt releasing as it was supposed to. I am in process of calling the company to obtain a new switch which certainly hope works more reliably.
justification: The incident resulted in no injury, but the potential for harm was high due to the chainsaw not shutting off when the trigger was released.

incident_description:
This report is regarding a Toro leaf blower which caught fire without any human interaction with it for the previous 36 hours.  The fire was spontaneous.

I had bought this leafblower in September 2014 from Lowe's.  The fire occurred on October 13, 2015.  So the blower was relatively new.

Early on October 12, 2015 I used the blower to clear off my back patio and walkways.  They are concrete.  As it was Fall with continuing leaves falling, I left the blower plugged in and sitting on its coiled extension cord on the concrete walkway, underneath a nearby redwood tree.  Weather was clear and warm for those and following days.

About 30 hours later I was away from home when a neighbor called me to tell me that there was "a large fire" underway in my back yard and that I should get there immediately.  When I returned, two neighbors had broken the gate to my yard to gain access and had extinguished two fires with a garden hose.  One was the blower itself, the other was in the redwood tree above.  They were alerted to the fire in my back yard by a pillar of dense, black smoke about 50 feet high.

Damaged were the blower, its extension cord, the concrete walkway, the adjoining railroad tie wall and the overhanging redwood tree.  The blower was a pile of burned plastic surrounding the metal of the blower motor, with the protruding nozzle not fully burned.  The redwood tree had several lower branches wholly burned; the fire had been spreading upward into the tree and its two neighbors before the fire was extinguished.

I phoned Toro to report the fire.  They were responsive, having a "Senior Paralegal" phone me.  I then dealt solely with her over the coming weeks.  She and Toro were very forthcoming in reimbursing me for the damages incurred -- $650.  I am satisfied with this reimbursement.

However, in the course that first phone call, I asked the paralegal if Toro would be reporting this fire to the CPSC.  She seemed startled at that question and didn't answer for several seconds.  She then stammered out "Well, why should we?"

I then told her that the CPSC kept databases of all such hazardous consumer product problems, and building that database depended upon knowledge of such events.  She tried to deflect this by saying that "Of course, Toro will track incidences and inform the CPSC if we find a pattern of problems with a product".

I told her that I would be reporting the incident even if Toro did not.  She asked "Why?"  I told her that this fire did result in minor property damage, could have resulted in the major loss of my house by fire if not taken care of by neighbors, and could actually could have caused a loss of life.

So I am reporting this.  

Two other things that the Toro representative told me raised my concerns.  First she tried to make it seem like leaving the blower plugged in was a major mistake on my part.  I told her that even at that moment I had at least 15 devices in my house plugged into power outlets.  Products needed to not ignite when plugged in to AC outlets.

The second was when I told her I had left the blower inside my garage at times, also plugged in.  She seemed surprised a blower would be inside a structure.  I told her that I, and countless others, used their products to blow out garages.

My belief is that the fire was caused when the blower spontaneously turned on, overheated, and then ignited.  About three feet down the adjoining wall you can see soot marks where the blower nozzle had been blowing soot while running.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and while it's possible for such an event to occur, it's not likely to happen frequently.

My extension cord was destroyed/melted and I threw it away.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant risk with the leaf blower overheating and causing a fire in the extension cord.

I went to get the fuel can and when I turned around the mower was in flames and completely engulfed. The flames were so high and the fire was so large, I had to call the fire department.

incident_description:
I was using an electric Craftsman leaf blower, Model 358.748260, to clear fallen leaves from landscaped areas in my yard.  It caught fire, with the fire burning where the prongs plug in to the cord. Within a minute I was able to disconnect the unit, at which time the flames were extinguished.  Both the blower and cord are no longer usable.  In researching this issue online, I found that other Craftsman electric leaf blower models have been recalled.  We purchased this unit directly from Sears in 2007, and used it only briefly every Fall to clean up fallen leaves in our yard.  I contacted Sears Home Service and their representative told me that this model has not been recalled.

Based on my experience, this Craftsman leaf blower model should be recalled, due to potential fire hazard as a result of only light use.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a fire, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' case, and the likelihood of occurrence is 'possible' given the online reports of similar issues with other Craftsman models.

incident_description:
I purchased a Kenmore 4 Burner plus side burner LPG Grill (P/N 307010030) manufactured by Char-Broil from Sears on 3/7/12. At the beginning of itÃÂs third grilling season, Spring of 2015, I put some pieces of chicken on the upper rack to slow bake using the two end burners on low. The temperature was reading about 350 degree F. After about ten or fifteen minutes, I went inside to answer a phone call. I returned a few minutes later to find the grill and the side of my house ablaze. 
Severe and unexpected corrosion/rusting of interior parts had deposited a heavy layer of rust and rusted metal debris covering the drip pan and causing fat to accumulate, rather than be conducted to the center drip cup and removed. A large hole had rusted through along the back edge of the pan, through which an updraft intensified the flames as they blew out the gap between the back edge of the cover and the rear top edge of the firebox, quickly igniting the wooden siding of the building. 
I filed a complaint with Char Broil. Customer service requested photos, and more photos, but three months later, has not settled my case. In fact, it is no longer accessible to customer service, who claimed it has been removed from their system to ÃÂcorporateÃÂ. I believe this product is poorly designed and manufactured, and is a severe fire hazard, and a danger to the public.
justification: The grill's severe corrosion led to a fire that could have caused injury or property damage, making it likely to occur again.

incident_description: We awoke this morning to a very strong smell of propane gas. While covering the Weber Genesis E330 grill on the deck yesterday after use we apparently bumped one of the burner controls, turning it on. Gas was emitted all night. A spark, perhaps a static spark from clothing, could have touched off an explosion and fire. This is the second time this has occurred. We believe that the burner controls are too easily turned on in such a situation and are extremely dangerous. We believe that there should be a positive stop of the controls in the off position that would require some explicit action to overcome. This event, and the previous occurrence, scared us deeply. We believe this to be a design flaw and a very serious safety risk.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the potential for an explosion and fire was high due to the continuous emission of propane gas, making it an incident with a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description: I purchased a Brunton propane stove a couple years ago and the gas hose leaked from the over-pressure valve. Primus, the parent company sent me a replacement stove, a Primus Profile and hose. I was about to use the stove 2 days ago in below freezing temperatures in [REDACTED]. When I screwed the propane cylinder onto the hose, the over-pressure valve failed and a jet of propane came shooting out - same problem as with the first stove. It's pretty clear that the hose assembly has a sacrificial part in the over-pressure valve and that this part fatigues and eventually fails. Under normal use, the valve freezes due to the expanding propane gas, and my guess is that these freeze-thaw cycles are what fatigue the part and lead to failure. If someone were to leave the hose attached to the cylinder while they were camping, the valve could fail and fill a car or camper with propane. In addition, if the valve fails while cooking, the jet of propane could easily reach the flame of the stove about 2 feet away. I have the second hose that failed if you need to examine it
justification: The incident has already occurred twice, indicating a high likelihood of recurrence.

I have a Wolfgang Puck 5 in 1 Grill/Griddle with Dual Temp Controls ModelBCGL1000.  I have used it less than 20x and this last time towards the end of cooking it turned off on its own which it had never done in the past.  I reached for the plug to unplug and plug it back in and jumped my hand back as it was so hot it nearly burned my hand.  I had to get a towel to unplug it from the socket.  The plug and wire were hot as well as the wall socket.  

My boyfriend checked it a while later, plugging it in and turning it on, it normally beeps when plugged in however it didn't beep nor turn on at all.  This not only hurt my hand due to how hot it was but had the potential to start a dangerous electrical fire.  It seems that this company did not rectify the problem from the previous model in which it had to recall 27,000 models.  

I contacted the Manager of the Warranty Department at Wolfgang Puck, [REDACTED], expressing my concerns as well as the similarities in this new model with what seems to be the same type of fire hazard potential.  She responded with an email but her voicemail was even more concerning.  She "there is no way, I can guarantee this is a fire hazard".  She also stated "with your unit there is nothing wrong with that.....you stated that the plug gets so hot um it will get a little hot definitely but keep in mind it is a grounded plug so it will NOT get hot enough where it will catch a fire or any type of fire hazard as concerned".

The company seems to be disregarding this potential safety hazard, even though a similar one occurred, with a similar model just a couple of years prior.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (burnt hand) and had the potential for a dangerous electrical fire.

incident_description:
Stihl chainsaw 362 has fuel cap which does not reliably seal fuel tank resulting in spilled fuel on operators leg (pants). Although annoying this could result  in a fire if near an ignition source. i have had problems with these "flip style" caps in the past - on other Stihl models. This most recent saw had a cap that would not seal after many diliberate attampts to insert and close the mechanism carefully. The leakage resulting from these poorly performing fuel caps could result in an unessacary burn to the saw operator leg. A similar Stihl fuel cap has been the subject of a recall on other types of Sthil power equipment, chainsaws for some reason, were not included. These Sthil "flip type" fuel and oil caps are not reliably capable of preventing a fuel spill onto the operator and also into the environment. A saw fully fueled and left to sit on the ground could conceivably discharge the contents of the tank over - say - a lunch break. Problems with these caps have been ongoing for many years and are well know within the industry  - a Google search of Stihl fuel caps returns some discussion of the shortcomings of this overly complex and fragile design. Screw type fuel caps have been successfully used for decades on many types of equipment requiring a fuel tank and a cap used for sealing the tank. The principles and utility of a screw cap are well understood. Common sense could lead one to believe that Sthil's "flip type" caps have not proven themselves - to be able to be used correctly - as Stihl may assert - and or  to reliably retain the contents of the fuel and oil tanks. A Gooogle search, today, of "Stihl fuel caps burns"- returned a report by the National Interagency Fire Center, of a wildland firefighter burned from gasoline soaked chaps. The report is - Subject: Stihl Chainsaw Fuel/Oil Caps  Date 08/01/2014.
The warning issued in this "Safety Warning Final" is a plausible occurrence given my experience with fuel leakage on my pants. 
So this issue is well know, over a period of many years and now one could presume at least one person injured .
justification: Fuel leakage from the unreliable 'flip style' fuel cap could lead to an operator burn if near an ignition source, as evidenced by a reported incident involving a wildland firefighter.

One of our employees was using a Werner PS-48 4 ft Portable Scaffold.  He was applying drywall mud with the wheels locked.  The unit broke apart and the employee fell 3' to the floor.  The diagonal bracing broke away from the center piece on the back side of the scaffold.  It appears the metal in the center piece is too thin to handle the type of use it's designed for.  A check of 4 other Werner PS-48's showed one unit about to fail for the same reason and two of the units with stress cracks in the same area.  

We believe these scaffolds have a faulty design and we have pulled them from the field.
justification: Injury occurred due to faulty design of the scaffold, and multiple units showing signs of failure indicate high likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description:
At the beginning of September 2015, I purchased a Task Light, Energizer TUF2AAPEW UPN-135030 104-68520-1.

The case became extremely hot. I checked the batteries (which were included) and they were properly installed.

I called the service contact, 800-383-7323. The representative said there was not need for me to do anything further; they would send me a voucher to replace the defective product. I recycled the batteries and disposed of the light.

Last week I redeemed the voucher for one light and then bought a second unit. Neither of these units worked. Apparently the switches are defective, sometimes the lights work, sometimes they don't.

Now I'm not only feeling foolish, but also concerned. I called the consumer number this morning. "[REDACTED]" told me I should send them pictures of the lights and their packaging as this would be proof of purchase, and they would then send me vouchers.

I told her I was more concerned that the lights are defective and a safety issue and should be examined by Energizer. She said that wasn't their policy; they don't have anyone to do that. I tried to explain that there could be a burn or fall hazard, but she insisted there was nothing to be done.

I told her I wasn't interested in vouchers because I certainly wasn't going to buy this item again, and if they did not want to examine the lights, I felt I had to try to alert a consumer agency about the issue.

Our conversation was courteous on both sides. I would appreciate your letting me know if I have reported this to the proper place, and if not, where I should.

Thank you for your time.
justification: While no injuries were reported, the incident involved multiple defective products with potential safety hazards, such as overheating and unpredictable functionality.

incident_description:
I was using a RYOBI 2 cycle gas trimmer with bush trimming attachment.  The plastic fuel line from the gas tank to the engine disconnected and the gas leaked out and caught fire.  My right hand had a glove which caught fire (which was holding the trimmer on the handle next to the fuel tank), the right side of my short sleeve shirt caught fire, and my right arm sustained second degree burns.

I was able to put fire out with fire extinguisher, and removed glove and shirt before I sustained more extensive burns.

This fuel line disconnecting was a recurrent problem.  Before this occurred, I had just filled the tank and carefully re-attached the fuel line.  However, there is no clamp that secures the plastic fuel line to the male receptacle on the engine that would help prevent this small plastic fuel line from disconnecting.
justification: The incident resulted in second degree burns, and the issue of the fuel line disconnecting was recurrent, indicating a possible design flaw.

incident_description:
I was using my Toro Model 51575 Leaf Blower/Vacumn for yard cleanup on 10/29/15 as shown in the operating manual when it essentially exploded.  The impeller inside flew apart, the motor came loose and pieces of the impeller penetrated through the exterior housing of the leaf blower.  At the time I was holding it against my thighs and the impact felt like I was hit by two large rubber bands on the inside of each thigh.  If I had been holding it a couple inches high (crotch level) I would still be vomiting blood (as any guy who has been hit with a baseball in the crotch can attest).  If the pieces of the impeller had hit me it would have neutered me.  Laugh if you will but it wouldn't be funny if it happened to you.
I reported it to [REDACTED] at Toro and he took the report.  He told me his boss wanted to talk to me and would call me back in an hour or so.  He referred to his boss as a "her".  After waiting around much of the afternoon without being called, I'm not happy.  I narrowly averted a serious injury and then I was stood up on my return phone call.
[REDACTED] gave me a case [REDACTED]
justification: The incident involved a severe malfunction of the leaf blower, with the impeller flying apart and pieces penetrating the exterior, posing a high risk of injury.

incident_description:
STEPPED ON THE OPEN LID OF THE CART, CAUSING THE CART TO FALL AND PULL ME AGAINST THE RIDGE OF THE CART. HIT MY LEFT CHEEK BONE CAUSING A GASH THAT REQUIRED STITCHES. 

(FULL EXPLANATION ATTACHED IN EMAIL SENT ON MARCH 27, 2015 TO THE PRESIDENT & CEO OF REHRIG PACIFIC, MANUFACTURER OF THIS CART)

Text of the consumer's e-mail dated March 27, 2015 addressed to the officials of Rehrig Pacific:

I am writing this email to you in regards to the 95 gallon compost Yardy bin that is contracted to the city of Cedar Rapids through your company.
On Saturday, March 21, 2015 at approximately 4:30pm I was raking my yard and depositing the debris into the Yardy. I was using a shovel as a scoop and a rake, clamping them together as we have a large yellow lab that I was also cleaning up after and I don't like to touch any of it with my hands. The Yardy was on my left and as I turned to empty the contents of my clamped debris into the open Yardy my foot caught the lid. The momentum caused by the heavy lid allowing the Yardy to fall immediately pulled me forward . Off balanced now by the rolling bin, I fell sideways and turned my head. The opposite side of the bin hit my left cheek bone causing a gash.
It all happened so fast! It was like stepping onto a skateboard. I immediately went to St. Lukes ER, located about 15 minutes from my house. I received 7 stitches, a very bruised and swollen left side of my face, and a very sore neck from the force of the impact. 6 days later, as I write this to you my face is still swollen and tender and my neck is still very sore. It is hard to turn my head to the left without considerable pain. I will also have a permanent scar on my left cheek.
After explaining to the nurse what happened, she nodded knowingly and said,"Yes, we see a lot of these injuries." What?!! I couldn't imagine more than just one or two people being hurt. But then I remembered my sister in law also had broken her fingers while moving her Yardy (with the lid closed).
Just on a whim, I Googled "Yardy Accidents in Cedar Rapids" and I found an article "Attack of the Yardys" featured in our local Gazette. Many people have been hurt. The article did not specify whether all accidents had happened when the lid was open and moving. It implied many did. My accident was not caused by me actively moving it. The low hanging (9" off the ground) is easy to catch your foot on, the lid also makes it top heavy and on the very same side are large wheels. The design makes absolutely no sense to me. I will no longer be using my Yardy while my children and their friends are playing in the backyard, as one of them may come to talk to me and innocently run into it or run into it with a bike tire. Now I know that is all it takes for that top heavy, tall, hard plastic on wheels to tip and cause a serious injury.
I'm aware I am not the only one. I would like to know what are your plans to improve on this design.

I have attached a pictured of my injury before the stitches and after.
justification: Injury occurred due to the cart's design, and the incident was likely due to the cart's low height and top-heavy nature.

incident_description:

incident_description:
We purchased a Honda 21 inch deck EZ Start 3N1 mower on May 1, 2015.  We used it all summer with the bag attached and with the lever in the "mulch" position.  On the date of injury, I switched the lever to the "bag" position.  As I was mowing, the bag apparently flew off the mower, hitting me in the left leg and causing me to trip over the bag.  I say "apparently" because one moment I was mowing and the next thing I knew I was face down on the ground.  When I stood up, I saw that the left leg of my jeans was soaked through with blood.  My husband took me to the nearest ER, where I received 18 surface stitches, plus numerous "mattress" stitches because of the depth of the laceration.  The cut is approximately 4 1/2 inches long and is located about 3 inches below my knee.  The ER doctor said that I can expect a nasty scar.

When we returned home, my husband found the grass bag on the ground approximately two yards behind the spot where the self-propelled mower had come to a stop.
justification: Injury occurred due to mower bag detachment, likely due to improper lever positioning, indicating high likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description:
The product in question is the GREENWORKS 40-VOLT 20" DUAL-BLADE Li-ION BATTERY-POWERED LAWNMOWER, MODEL 25302.

I bought this lawnmower, serial number GWT0510399-02/20/14, through Target Stores (on-line mail order, with order number 102506043369) on April 30, 2015.  When the lawnmower developed a serious safety problem (see below), a similar replacement lawnmower (Model 25302) was sent to me by Greenworks' post-sales support representative, Sunrise Global Marketing Inc., in June 2015.  The serial number of the replacement unit is GWT0510445-02/20/14. 

The total area of my lawn (total of front and back) is about 4,800 square feet.  This area is flat, except for a steep slope on one side of the front yard.  

I used the first lawnmower (above) several times, with no problem.  However, on or about May 21, 2015, I noticed that the bail was repeatedly failing to electrically disconnect the electric motor when the bail was released.  (The bail is the safety bar that must be kept depressed in order to maintain an electrical connection to the motor.)  When the bail is released, it is supposed to disconnect the electric motor.  Failure to disconnect is a SERIOUS SAFETY PROBLEM because, in the event that the lawnmower starts to slide back toward the user on a slope, the electric motor must be quickly stopped to prevent extreme injury.  When release of the bail fails to stop the electric motor, the only way to stop the motor is to manually pull out the circuit key, or manually pull out the battery, either of which takes a number of seconds to perform.  

I called the Greenworks support representative, Sunrise Global Marketing (telephone 888-909-6757) and explained the safety problem to them.  They made arrangements for a replacement unit (see above for the S/N) to be sent to me through their office in Mooresville, NC (telephone 704-660-2800).  I received the replacement unit on June 9, 2015.  The Sunrise Global Marketing reference number for this transaction is 1133884.  During June, July, and August, I used the replacement unit several times with no safety problem.  

Then, on September 19, 2015, while I was mowing my lawn, the replacement unit repeatedly displayed the same safety problem as the original unit: RELEASE OF THE BAIL WOULD NOT STOP THE ELECTRIC MOTOR.  

On September 19, 2015, I called Sunrise Global Marketing at telephone 888-909-6757, and also the retailer, Target Stores, and reported the latest safety problem.  I sought to return the lawnmower and obtain a refund.  Both organizations advised me that the lawnmower could not be returned.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the repeated failure of the bail to disconnect the motor poses a significant safety risk, making it an incident.

incident_description:
I purchased a Gorilla brand 3 cubic foot garden dump cart from Home Depot.  I took it back to my home where I was assembling it inside of my garage.  The smell from the thing was awful but I wanted to get it done.  Eventually my wife told me that everyone was ready to go eat and that I needed to finish it later.  As I got into the car, I began to feel suddenly ill with nausea.  We got to the restaurant and I was so nauseated I couldn't order and in fact couldn't stay in the restaurant.  I also began feeling light-headed in the restaurant so I went outside.  By the time my family finished eating, I was finally shaking off some of the light-headedness and the nausea was not as bad.  
Upon getting home, I was feeling healthy again, still a little nauseated, and getting back into the garage with the product definitely began setting off the illness again.

I believe the odor remaining on the cart was the cause of my sudden symptoms and I worry that had I not been pulled away from it by my wife, that I could have passed out in the garage and continued inhaling the fumes and possibly be injured from fall or inhalation.

I am a physician, and the suddenness of the symptom onset and resolution make me think that exposure is the definite cause.  This product needs to off-gas more before being packaged and sold.  I am a very healthy 30yo.  A person who is not as fortunate in their health or in their proximity to others could be seriously inured.

Amazon reviews for the product are very significant for similar complaints.
http://www.amazon.com/Gorilla-Carts-GOR200B-Pneumatic-600-Pound/product-reviews/B0026RGNJ2/ref=cm_cr_pr_viewopt_kywd?sortBy=helpful&reviewerType=all_reviews&formatType=all_formats&filterByStar=all_stars&pageNumber=1&filterByKeyword=smell
justification: Potential for injury due to fainting and inhaling fumes, given the sudden onset and resolution of symptoms, and similar complaints in Amazon reviews.

incident_description:

The consumer's husband heard a pop and a hissing noise while he was inside of the house. The consumer's husband came outside to check on the grill and noticed that the grill was on fire.

The consumer's husband quickly yanked out the gas tank from the grill and put out fire with extinguisher. The consumer stated that the attachment in the grill that was connected to the tank was leaking gas.

The consumer's husband was able to avoid a more serious explosion by removing the gas tank. The consumer stated that the stainless steel panels and the top of the grill is scorched. The plastic control knobs are melted and do not work.

The consumer contacted Nexgrill to see if they can get replacement parts for the grill. The consumer was informed that they did not have anything available to provide them. 

The consumer's husband bought a hose from Amazon but it did not work on their grill. The consumer was able to get a refund for the hose from Amazon.

The grill does not work anymore.

The grill does not appear to be recalled.

incident_description: I have been using a Black & Decker GH1000 string trimmer for a couple of years.On numerous occasions it has damaged objects close to the vegetation being trimmed due to the string releasing unexpectedly. the damage is caused by both the sudden increase in the length of the string and the pieces of string cut off by the trimmer blade. I have received numerous small cuts to my legs from flying string fragments over the past couple or years. He is reporting this riding mower as a severe fire and explosion hazard.

incident_description: I had a gas leak coming from the bottom of the gas tank on my Cub Cadet Riding mower. The gas tank is held on by four bolts screwed into the tank from underneath the gas tank. The tank had several cracks around one of the bolts causing a slow leak and fumes of gasoline in my garage. These fumes could have been dangerous. A fire from the fumes could have burned my house down. I contacted Cub Cadet and asked if the manufacturer had a recall on the gas tank. The technical support department said no recall on my product. My incident number with Cub Cadet was [REDACTED]. I explained that their is a design defect in the bracketing of the gas tank. The vibration of the machine caused the cracking on the bottom of the gas tank. All Cub Cadet would do for me, was to sell me a new gas tank. I believe the tank should have a rubber cushion washer under the tank to prevent the tank from cracking and causing the leak. This is a poor design and potentially dangerous to anyone with this machine.
justification: Gas leak from cracked tank could have caused a fire, posing a significant risk to the house and occupants.

incident_description: I replaced the original burner on my [REDACTED] [REDACTED]Bar-B-Que about 18 months ago with a Grill Mark stainless steel BAR burner. Part Number 81282 which I purchased at the local ACE hardware. I was cooking on the Bar-B-Que when suddenly the outside of the BBQ was engulfed in flames. Turning off the gas by using the burner control knobs on the front of the BBQ stopped the flames. There were no injuries or property damage. The burner was a "universal" burner so they used an accordion type gas pipe between the burner control and the burner. This type of gas pipe was used so it could be bent to fit any type of Bar-B-Que. Upon inspection I found that the gas pipe had broke at the connection on the bottom of the burner.
